newsitem.title: GERMANY: European car market set for choppy recovery.
newsitem.headline: European car market set for choppy recovery.

text.p: The European car market is set for a choppy but certain recovery over the next three years, moving toward unit sales levels not seen since the early part of this decade, industry analysts said on Monday.

Speaking at a car industry conference, DRI/McGraw-Hill analysts said European government incentive programmes could distort the size of the European market, boosting sales by 2.2 percent this year before contributing to flat growth in 1998.
"Only after 1999 do we expect the European car market to recover to a classical pattern of demand," said Christophe Laborde, analyst at the DRI Automotive Group.
Car output in Europe, he said, should climb to around 14 million units by 2001, the highest since 1990. Unit car sales were expected to be near 13 million units in 1997.

DRI said underlying demand should get a boost in the coming years from several fronts including the introduction of new models, improving consumer confidence and increased competition which promises to cap prices.
DRI echoed the view of other industry analysts that German carmaker Volkswagen AG should turn in the best performance in the coming few years.
"The VW group and the brand will be the clear winners in the 1990s," Laborde said, adding models such as the new Golf would boost demand.
Others such as Renault got more gloomy forecasts in the face of a weak domestic market and stiff competition from new models. "1997 and 1998 will be tough times for the French," he said.
At the root of uneven demand across are government fiscal incentive programmes in Italy, France and Spain to get old cars off the road.
DRI forecasts that an Italian scheme will boost demand there by 18 percent in 1997. Next year, however, after the programme has expired, demand should shrink by 14 percent.
A similar scheme in France boosted demand by 10.5 percent last year, but the withdrawal of state support would lead to a sharp decline this year, DRI said.
Only in Spain, where the scrapping programme is permanent, did DRI expect a sustained increase in demand.

A new emission tax in Germany should spur replacement demand from the third quarter of this year, as will demand for cars from people who first bought new vehicles shortly after German unification in 1990, DRI said.
